tagline.text: An emerald crater lake left by a 20th-century mega-eruption

children.text: A volcano whose summit collapsed in one of the 20th century's largest eruptions in
, leaving a caldera now filled with an emerald-green lake. Ride a 4x4 jeep across a canyon of hardened volcanic ash (lahar), then trek up a riverbed to look down over the crater lake.
Mount Pinatubo is a stratovolcano rising at the border of Tarlac, Zambales, and Pampanga provinces. Dormant for over 500 years, it erupted on
in what became the second-largest terrestrial volcanic eruption of the 20th century. The eruption caused the entire summit to collapse, lowering the mountain's height from about
above sea level to around
, and creating a massive caldera roughly
2.5km
across. Ash and sulfur dioxide that shot up into the stratosphere had a global effect, cooling the Earth's average temperature by about 0.5°C over the following one to two years.

After the eruption, rainwater collected in the caldera to form today's Pinatubo crater lake. The water, laced with dissolved volcanic minerals, shifts between emerald, teal, and jade depending on the sunlight, standing out vividly against the grey cliffs that surround it. The route to the lake is itself spectacular. The vast grey sand plains and canyons carved dozens of meters deep, formed as ash and debris flows (lahar) from the eruption hardened, look like a scene from another planet.

The Pinatubo area is home to the Aeta, an indigenous Filipino people. The eruption wiped out many Aeta villages and forced people to relocate, and today they make a living driving 4x4s, guiding, and working in tourism services. The lake is also considered sacred by the Aeta community, so activities such as swimming are restricted.

The route most travelers use starts from Sta. Juliana in Capas, Tarlac, riding a 4x4 across the lahar fields before hiking up along a riverbed. The physical demands are moderate, so even those without much hiking experience can manage it comfortably, making it a good recommendation for travelers interested in geology and natural history, or expats who want to give visiting family or guests from Korea a special day out.
Ride a jeep for about
1–1.5 hours
from Sta. Juliana across the ash plains around Crow Valley and the O'Donnell River. Crossing waterways and cresting sand dunes is a thrilling experience in itself.
From where the 4x4 drops you off, hike up about
5–7km
over
1.5–2 hours
. Most of it is gentle sand and gravel, crossing shallow streams several times. Walking between massive boulders and sheer ash cliffs is the highlight of the scenery.
Look down over the caldera lake from the viewpoint at the end of the trek. The water shows its most vivid emerald color around
10 AM
, when the sunlight is strong.
You can see textbook volcanic terrain firsthand: spots where steam rises and sulfur can be smelled, layered ash cross-sections, and massive boulders flung out during the eruption.

blocks.title: Meet an Aeta village and its culture

children.text: On the way, you'll pass through an Aeta community village, where an indigenous guide can share stories about the eruption. Be respectful and ask permission before taking photos.

blocks.title: Mud spa or hot spring after the descent

children.text: Some tours offer an optional volcanic-ash mud spa or hot spring on the way back. A great way to ease the fatigue from trekking.

blocks.title: Climbing to the crater ridge via the Inararo route

children.text: A new route that enters by 4x4 from Inararo village in Porac, Pampanga, and climbs about
5.8km

one way past Ana-an Falls. It is harder than the Kapas route, with many sections of scrambling over rocks and crossing streams, but you can look down on the lake from the crater ridge, and foreigners can join without an Air Force visit permit.

Since temperatures rise sharply after midday and the risk of afternoon showers increases, tour operators schedule things so the descent finishes around noon.
From Manila, take NLEX up and switch to SCTEX, then exit at Concepcion and head toward Capas. From Capas town, it's about
20km
of country road west to Sta. Juliana. It takes about
3–3.5 hours
from Manila, or about
1–1.5 hours
from Clark. There's parking around the Sta. Juliana registration office.
From Cubao or Pasay, take a bus (Victory Liner, Five Star, etc.) bound for Tarlac, Santa Ignacia, or Ilocos and get off at Capas. It's about
2.5–3 hours
, with fares around
. From Capas to Sta. Juliana, it's about
40 minutes–1 hour
by tricycle or chartered vehicle, about

per vehicle. Making the pre-dawn registration time would mean catching a bus in the middle of the night, which isn't easy, so a tour package is more realistic for travelers relying on public transport.

Clark International Airport (CRK), with direct flights from Korea, is the closest. It's most convenient to stay in Clark or Angeles and take a pre-dawn pickup tour. Tours departing from Clark or Manila, bundling transport, 4x4, guide, entrance fee, and lunch, are sold for about
per person.
Peak season is the dry season,
December–April
December–February
has cool dawns and clear skies, when the lake's water looks its most beautiful.
March–April
has clear skies too, but the lahar plains reflect the sun so strongly that the midday heat index can reach 40°C, making an early start and plenty of water essential.
During the
June–October

wet season, upstream rain can swell the lahar river in an instant, and with the risk of debris flows, tours are often suspended or closed for extended periods. When a typhoon warning or heavy rain is forecast, authorities ban entry, so a wet-season visit isn't recommended.
November
and
May
sit on the boundary between dry and wet seasons, so it's best to decide flexibly based on the weather.

Pinatubo is still classified as an active volcano. If the Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (PHIVOLCS) raises the alert level, entry is immediately restricted, so check the alert status before you set off.
The Kapas route had all tourism suspended from
over an issue of ancestral domain rights of the Aeta community, and reopened on

. Also, Crow Valley, which the 4x4s pass through, is an Air Force firing range, so trekking is sometimes halted for several days during the annual spring US-Philippine joint exercise (Balikatan). If you are going in spring, be sure to check with the tour operator before departing whether it is operating.

The most realistic way to make the pre-dawn registration is to stay the night before in Clark or Angeles. The Clark Freeport Zone and Angeles area offer everything from budget-to-midrange hotels at about
a night to resort-style hotels at
or more, and it's about
1–1.5 hours
by car from Clark to Sta. Juliana. There are also modest lodges and homestays around Capas and Sta. Juliana, so arriving and staying the night before lets you start out with the most ease.

There's no shop along the trek, so bring snacks and water. On the way back, be sure to try the food of Pampanga, known as the "culinary capital of the Philippines." Angeles is the birthplace of sisig, chopped pig's head sizzled on a hot plate, and the old restaurants known as its originators are still thriving. Burong kanin, a tangy fermented rice side dish, and tocino, sweet cured pork, are also Pampanga's pride.
The registration cutoff is set for an early pre-dawn hour. Being late may make same-day entry impossible, so be sure to keep to your tour operator's meeting time.
There are many stream crossings along the trekking section. Wear trekking sandals that can get wet, or quick-drying running shoes.
The 4x4 section is very dusty with volcanic ash. Bring a mask or buff and sunglasses, and keep your camera in a ziplock bag.
Bring at least 2 liters of water per person, electrolyte drinks, and energy bars. Long stretches have almost no shade, so fluid loss is high.
A wide-brimmed hat, a long-sleeve rash guard, and sunscreen are essential. The lahar sand reflects sunlight, and your face and neck can burn easily.
Photos of the lake come out most vivid around
. The water looks murky when it's cloudy, so wait a bit at the viewpoint if needed.
The registration office accepts cash only. Withdraw money in advance at an ATM in Capas town.
A tip for the 4x4 driver and guide (about
per person) isn't required, but it's customary.

Those aged 60 and over should bring a paper medical certificate saying they are fit to hike or a travel insurance policy covering outdoor activities, and children are accepted only from age 6 or 7 depending on the operator. Those aged 40–59 may have their blood pressure taken on site.

Since the reopening, the Kapas route is in principle booked only through operators accredited by the local government. Before booking, check whether the tour fee includes the 4x4, guide, environmental fee, and Botolan fees.

Swimming and entering the crater lake are prohibited. This is strictly enforced due to the volcanic mineral content, sudden depth changes, and its status as a sacred site for the indigenous community.
Foreigners need a Philippine Air Force (PAF) visit permit to take the Kapas route.
You must submit your passport photo page through an accredited operator at least 35 days before your visit

, and if you go without a permit, you will be turned back at the registration desk. This applies to travelers of every nationality, so if your schedule is tight, consider the Inararo route, which needs no permit.
During the wet season or right after rain, the lahar river can suddenly rise. If your guide gives the order to withdraw, follow it immediately.
The stairs and path down to the lakeshore are sometimes closed or restricted depending on the period. Don't go past the safety line at the viewpoint.
Always hold onto the handrail while the 4x4 is moving, and don't lean your body outside the vehicle. The jolts are severe on rough sections.
Heatstroke and dehydration at midday are the most common incidents. If you have a cardiovascular condition or are older, don't push yourself, and rest well partway through.
When passing through an Aeta community village, don't hand out candy or money to children indiscriminately. If you want to help, use an official community program instead.
